title: Gmail's Gemini integration was cluttering my inbox, but I turned it off with a single toggle
excerpt: Google forced Gemini into Gmail by default, but you don't have to live with the clutter. Here is how to safely turn it off
content_html:
Published Sep 19, 2026, 8:30 AM EDT

Jesse is a lifelong technology enthusiast who has been exploring smartphones and mobile tech for more than two decades. He began his career in IT consulting and project management before making a career change into tech journalism in 2007 with iLounge. During that time, he authored three editions of iPod & iTunes Portable Genius for Wiley Publishing and has since written for iDrop News, Lifewire, SlashGear, and Digital Trends.

While Jesse remains strongly immersed in the Apple ecosystem, you'll commonly find him rocking both an iPhone and a Pixel at the same time, where he likes to live on the edge with the latest iOS and Android betas. His tricked-out smart home also responds equally well to "Hey Siri," "Alexa", and "OK Google." His other hobbies include reading, curating his Plex library, and helping out at his local church with everything from live video production to governance. 

It may be hard to imagine today, but there was a time when Gmail was praised for its simple and elegant user interface that was a breath of fresh air from the alternatives.

I signed up in 2004, a few weeks after it launched. I've been all-in ever since. I even switched from a gmail.com address in January 2007 to embrace Google Apps for Your Domains (now known as Google Workspace).

That also means I've had a front-row seat to watch Google turn Gmail from a fast, lightweight web UI into a sea of clutter.

To be fair, Google has added some welcome user interface polish over the years, but things have started to go a little over the top as we've entered the Gemini era.

It's clear Google really wants people to use Gemini. It's forced it down everyone's throats, requiring those who don't want the clutter to opt out.

Fortunately, that's entirely doable — and it's not hard as long as you know which knobs to tweak, and you're willing to live without a few other "smart" features.

The Gemini overload

Gmail's smart features have spiraled out of control

We started down this slippery slope in 2017, long before generative AI was anything more than a gleam in Google's eye.

The first few drops over the dam were smart replies, a feature that came over from Google's tragically short-lived Inbox by Gmail project.

These were handy, and they got even better when Gemini supercharged them. However, it wasn't long before Google's AI tools began expanding through the rest of Gmail like a spiderweb.

From smart replies came summary cards at the top of email threads, persistent sidebar prompts, and intrusive suggestions offering its opinionated take on what my drafts should look like.

Google positioned this as a nice productivity boost, and perhaps for some people it was. For me, it was visual noise.

I don't need Gemini to "Help Me Write," thank you very much. I prefer to craft my own prose, and I can type a reply faster than I can read an AI suggestion.

It quickly started to feel like death by a thousand cuts. Tiny daily annoyances that added friction to simply going through my inbox and reading my email instead of hearing what Gemini thinks about it.

To be fair, I'm sure these features are useful for a lot of people. I'm not sure Google did the right thing by foisting them on everyone by default.

Freeing Gmail from the AI cruft

Make sure you turn off the right switch

Until a couple of years ago, one of the easiest workarounds was switching to Gmail's classic "basic HTML" interface. I used this a lot when dealing with Gemini began to irk me.

This mode had the nice side benefit of removing Gemini from the mix, along with other distractions, and speeding things up.

Sadly, Google killed that off in 2024. Now, everyone gets the standard UI — with the usual side helping of AI.

This means the only way to get Gemini out of Gmail now is to find the magic button to turn it off — and Google doesn't make this obvious.

You won't find a global off switch labeled "Gemini." Instead, Google wraps it up more coyly in a pair of "smart features" options, found by clicking the Gear icon in Gmail and choosing See all settings.

However, there's also a bit of a decoy hiding in here. On the General tab in your Gmail settings, you'll find a checkbox to Turn on smart features in Gmail, Chat, and Meet.

This checkbox is a blunt instrument. It not only disables Gemini, but also turns off everything from spelling and grammar to important mail notifications and automatic sorting of incoming messages into category tabs.

That's great if you don't want any of these features, but that's probably not what you're looking for.

If you want to get rid of the Gemini cruft without dumbing down your whole inbox, ignore that and go to the button below it instead: Manage Workspace smart feature settings.

Click this, and a pop-up window appears with the magic switch: Smart features in Google Workspace.

For Gmail, you only need to worry about the first one. Turn it off, and Gemini will vanish not only from Gmail but also from Chat, Drive, Meet, Docs, and Sheets.

This is an account-wide setting, so it will apply to the Gmail app on your mobile device as well — although it may take some time to propagate, so don't be worried if Gemini doesn't vanish right away.

The second toggle applies to "other" Google products outside the core productivity suite, such as Maps, Google Assistant, and Gemini.

You can also access these toggles from the Gmail settings on iOS or Android under Data privacy > Google Workspace smart features. Again, ignore the "Smart features" toggle — that's the same trap I mentioned earlier.

If you use a managed Google Workspace account for work or school, your organization controls these settings. If you can't find this button, reach out to your IT admin.

A breath of fresh air

Gemini won't completely vanish, but it will stay out of your way

After you've disabled Google Workspace smart features, your inbox should be free of Gemini's attempts to summarize your emails and help you write.

However, Gemini will still lurk among the icons in the upper-right corner of your screen, but it's effectively neutered when smart features are off.

Clicking it (or tapping it on your mobile) will prompt you to turn smart features back on. Just choose No thanks, and you'll be returned to your regularly scheduled inbox.

On the flip side, this makes it easy to change your mind if you decide you want Gemini's more advanced AI features.

And that's totally fair. The real issue isn't that advanced AI tools aren't valuable — they inarguably are for many people — but forcing them on by default needlessly complicates the user experience for those who don't even know what to do with them, much less actually want them.
